A good snack is easy to prepare, safe for everyone including people with allergies, and affordable. To design a snack, compare options with a short list of criteria: food groups, sugar and salt, cost and safety.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Compare two snacks using the criteria: (A) carrot sticks and hummus, (B) a chocolate bar. Which is better for an everyday snack, and why?

FEEDBACK
A is better: it gives vegetables and legumes, is low in sugar and gives fibre. B is a sometimes food with high added sugar and fat and few nutrients. Compare with criteria, not only taste.

WATCH FOR
Believing a snack is healthy because the packet says 'healthy' or 'natural'. Read the food groups and the ingredient list, because some labelled snacks are high in sugar.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Design a healthy snack for a class of 24 with an allergy-safe plan. Write the ingredients by group, a score using four criteria, a cost estimate and two safety steps for handling food. Prepare it only with an adult and wash hands first.

Write a short reflection naming one choice you changed and why. Any movement is optional, adult-supervised and can be done in a gentler way or described instead.

teach_steps.explain:
A healthy snack gives energy between meals and comes from the five food groups, such as fruit, vegetables with hummus, yoghurt, cheese and crackers, or plain popcorn. A good snack is easy to prepare, safe for everyone including people with allergies, and affordable. To design a snack, compare options with a short list of criteria: food groups, sugar and salt, cost and safety.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make safe, healthy and respectful choices using clear cues and reasons, rather than guessing or copying others. Every choice keeps bodies safe and includes everyone.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the cues, rules or choices that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. For any movement, use a clear space, ask an adult to be nearby, move at your own comfortable level and stop if anything hurts or feels unsafe. You may always choose a gentler version or only describe the movement. One deliberate, reasoned change is more useful than a longer answer.

teaching.feedback: The new situation should use the same PDHPE idea as the example, but happen in a different place or with different people.
teaching.fix: Change the choice or strategy, not just the wording.
teaching.guided_attempt: Describe or practise one fresh situation that uses the same skill and write a short reason for your choice.
teaching.misconception: Repeating the worked example cannot show transfer to a new situation.
teaching.model: A healthy snack gives energy between meals and comes from the five food groups, such as fruit, vegetables with hummus, yoghurt, cheese and crackers, or plain popcorn. A good snack is easy to prepare, safe for everyone including people with allergies, and affordable. To design a snack, compare options with a short list of criteria: food groups, sugar and salt, cost and safety. Now choose a different situation to show you can transfer the idea.
teaching.rule: Use the same PDHPE idea in a new place, game or situation, not a copy of the example. Review safety, fairness and inclusion.
teaching.why: This helps the learner make safe, healthy and respectful choices using clear cues and reasons, rather than guessing or copying others. Every choice keeps bodies safe and includes everyone.
